screens.title: Infrastructure as Code for CI/CD with CloudFormation & CDK
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on treating your CI/CD pipeline itself as code. Infrastructure as Code means you write machine-readable templates that create the very pipelines that build, test, and deploy your applications. You will see how CloudFormation templates define resources like CodeCommit repositories and CodeBuild projects, and how the AWS Cloud Development Kit lets you express the same infrastructure in familiar programming languages. This matters because pipelines that are versioned, reviewed, and deployed from code are reproducible, auditable, and safe to update. A concrete example is a CloudFormation template that creates a CodeCommit repo, an S3 artifacts bucket, an IAM role for builds, and a CodeBuild project with a buildspec provided inline. Common errors come from only putting application infra in IaC while keeping pipelines manual — that causes drift and hidden differences between environments. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to choose a tool, model a pipeline in code, use nested templates or constructs for reuse, and run drift detection to keep resources in sync. Start by comparing CloudFormation's declarative stacks with CDK's programmatic constructs and follow with hands-on templates and a CDK example.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on both declarative and programmatic IaC for CI/CD. First, you'll be able to define and manage AWS CI/CD resources like CodeCommit, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline using CloudFormation templates, which gives you a single source of truth for pipeline provisioning. Second, you'll use the AWS CDK to programmatically define pipelines and their infrastructure. CDK lets you write constructs in languages such as TypeScript or Python and synthesize CloudFormation, reducing boilerplate and improving reuse. Third, you'll implement advanced CloudFormation features such as nested stacks, change sets, and custom resources to build modular, safe pipeline automation. These features matter for safe updates and team workflows. Fourth, you'll migrate manually configured pipelines to IaC and detect drift so your deployed resources match the code. A common misconception is that IaC is only for servers; here we show why pipelines themselves must be managed as code. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify competency by deploying a small pipeline stack and running drift detection.

Module 02 › Chapter 2.5 › Skills & Milestones

Skills you will practice

screens.title: What is IaC for CI/CD?
screens.narratorSegment: Infrastructure as Code means expressing infrastructure and automation in machine-readable files so they can be versioned, reviewed, and deployed like software. For CI/CD this extends to the pipeline itself: repositories, build projects, artifact buckets, pipeline stages, and deploy applications are all resources you can manage in code. A clear example is writing a CloudFormation template that creates a CodeCommit repository, an S3 bucket for build artifacts, an IAM role, and a CodeBuild project with a buildspec. Treating these components as code provides repeatability — you can recreate the entire pipeline in a new account — and auditability because changes are visible in Git history. A common misconception is that IaC removes the need for operational review; instead, it shifts review earlier into code review, where change sets and approvals become important. Another contrast is between declaring resources in a static template versus programmatically generating them with CDK; both produce a final template, but CDK encourages reuse through constructs. Takeaway: model pipelines as first-class code artifacts and verify them with deployments and drift detection. How would you enforce a security baseline in every generated pipeline?

keyIdea.text: IaC for CI/CD means writing templates or constructs that create the pipeline resources so pipelines are reproducible and versioned.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.5 › IaC for CI/CD
Definition

Pipeline as Code

Describe pipeline resources in code so the pipeline lifecycle — create, update, delete — is executed by the IaC system, not manual clicks.

Concrete example
A CloudFormation template that provisions a CodeCommit repo, an S3 artifacts bucket, an IAM role, and a CodeBuild project with an inline buildspec.
Misconception
IaC does not remove governance; it centralizes configuration so code review, change sets, and drift detection enforce standards.
Key takeaway
Treat pipelines like software: version, review, and deploy them from code to keep environments consistent.
Analogy

Pipeline as a deployable service

Think of the pipeline as a service that you deploy with the same rigor as application services. The template is the service definition, and CloudFormation or CDK is the deployment engine.

Why it matters
  • Recreate pipelines in new accounts without manual steps.
  • Keep security guardrails in code and enforce them via reviews.
  • Detect drift to ensure deployed pipelines match templates.
Key Takeaway

Model pipelines as code and verify them with deployments and drift detection to avoid manual divergence.

screens.title: CloudFormation: Stacks and templates
screens.narratorSegment: CloudFormation lets you declare resources in YAML or JSON templates and manage them as a single unit called a stack. For CI/CD, a stack can include a CodeCommit repository, an S3 artifacts bucket, IAM roles, CodeBuild projects, and CodePipeline definitions. Each template describes the desired state; CloudFormation creates, updates, or deletes resources to match that state. Outputs expose useful values like a repository clone URL or a build project name for use in other stacks or scripts. A concrete example is the provided ci-cd-infra. yaml which creates a CodeCommit repo and a CodeBuild project with a buildspec. Intrinsic functions like reference and get-attribute connect resources inside a stack or nested stacks. A common misconception is that updating a template immediately changes resources; instead you submit a stack update or create a change set to preview changes. Use outputs and parameters to make templates reusable across environments, and prefer named IAM roles and least-privilege policies in templates to reduce risk. Closing question: what outputs would you expose to integrate a stack with another pipeline? CloudFormation: Stacks and templates means a cloudformation stack groups resources so you can manage the full pipeline lifecycle through template changes.. In practical terms, how templates, stacks, and outputs model ci/cd resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.5 › CloudFormation Stacks
Concept

Templates, stacks, and outputs

Templates declare resources; stacks apply the template to create an environment. Outputs expose values for other stacks or tooling.

Parameters
Allow environment-specific customization, like repository and bucket names.
Outputs
Return important values such as clone URLs and project names for integration.
Intrinsic functions
Use reference and get-attribute to connect resources within or across nested stacks.
Example
Resources:
  MyCodeBuildProject:
    Type: AWS::CodeBuild::Project
    Properties:
      Name: MyWebAppBuildProject
      ServiceRole: !GetAtt CodeBuildServiceRole.Arn
      Artifacts:
        Type: S3
        Location: !Ref BuildArtifactsBucket
      Environment:
        ComputeType: BUILD_GENERAL1_SMALL
        Image: aws/codebuild/amazonlinux2-x86_64-standard:4.0
      Source:
        Type: CODECOMMIT
        Location: !GetAtt MyCodeCommitRepo.CloneUrlHttp
This snippet shows a CodeBuild resource referencing a service role and an artifacts bucket through intrinsic functions.
Key Takeaway

Use parameters and outputs for reuse, and preview updates with change sets before applying them.

screens.title: Define a CodeBuild project in CloudFormation
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete CloudFormation definition of a CodeBuild project and explain the important properties. The template sets the project name, a service role for permissions, artifact configuration pointing to an S3 bucket, environment settings such as compute type and image, and a source block that references a CodeCommit repository. Intrinsic functions like get-attribute and reference connect resources: for example the project uses a service role ARN retrieved with get-attribute and points to the artifacts bucket using reference. An example buildspec is often provided either inline or as a file in the repository; this controls phases such as install and build. A common mistake is granting overly broad IAM policies in the service role; prefer policies that limit S3, CodeCommit, and CloudWatch actions to necessary resources. Concrete example: the ci-cd-infra. yaml includes a buildspec that installs dependencies, builds an index. html, and sets artifacts. Closing reflection: what minimal permissions does your build role need to produce and upload artifacts safely? content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.5 › CodeBuild Template
YAML Example
Resources:
  MyCodeBuildProject:
    Type: AWS::CodeBuild::Project
    Properties:
      Name: MyWebAppBuildProject
      ServiceRole: !GetAtt CodeBuildServiceRole.Arn
      Artifacts:
        Type: S3
        Location: !Ref BuildArtifactsBucket
      Environment:
        ComputeType: BUILD_GENERAL1_SMALL
        Image: aws/codebuild/amazonlinux2-x86_64-standard:4.0
        Type: LINUX_CONTAINER
      Source:
        Type: CODECOMMIT
        Location: !GetAtt MyCodeCommitRepo.CloneUrlHttp
        BuildSpec: buildspec.yml
Explainer
  • ServiceRole: Allows CodeBuild to read source, write artifacts, and publish logs; keep it least-privilege.
  • Artifacts: Point to an S3 bucket created in the same template or passed via parameter.
  • Environment: Choose compute type and image that match your build needs.
  • Source: CodeCommit location references the repo's clone URL via get-attribute.
Common mistake
Granting overly broad managed policies to the build role. Prefer specific S3, CodeCommit, and logs permissions.
Key Takeaway

Define and reference IAM roles and artifact locations in the template and validate permissions during review.

screens.title: Intrinsic Functions: !Ref and !GetAtt
screens.narratorSegment: Intrinsic functions are the glue inside CloudFormation templates that let one resource reference another. Two key functions used in CI/CD templates are reference and get-attribute. Use reference to retrieve a resource's logical name or parameter value, and use get-attribute to fetch properties such as an ARN or a clone URL. For example, a CodeBuild project's Artifacts Location can be set to the bucket name returned by reference, and the project's ServiceRole can be set using get-attribute to retrieve the role's ARN after it is created. These functions matter because they keep templates modular and allow nested stacks to share values without hard-coding names. A common confusion is expecting these functions to return runtime values visible before stack creation; instead they resolve during template processing by CloudFormation. Concrete example: the CodeBuild project snippet uses get-attribute for the role ARN and reference for the artifacts bucket. Takeaway: use intrinsic functions to wire resources together and keep templates reusable and environment-agnostic. What values would you expose from a nested stack to its parent? Intrinsic Functions: !Ref and !GetAtt means use reference and get-attribute to connect resources so templates remain modular and reusable.. In practical terms, connect resources inside templates and across nested stacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.5 › Intrinsic Functions
Concept

!Ref and !GetAtt

Reference returns a resource name or parameter; get-attribute returns a specific property such as an ARN or clone URL. They are resolved when CloudFormation processes the template.

When to use
Use reference for values like bucket names and get-attribute for properties not returned by reference, like role ARNs or resource endpoints.
Nested stacks
Expose outputs from child stacks and retrieve them in the parent using Fn::GetAtt or cross-stack references where supported.
Scenario
Suppose you have a nested template that creates a CodeCommit repository and returns its clone URL as an output. The parent stack can get that clone URL and pass it into a CodeBuild project's source location so builds know where to pull code.
Misconception
These functions are not runtime queries. They are template-level references resolved by CloudFormation during stack operations.
Key Takeaway

Use intrinsic functions to wire resources, expose outputs for reuse, and keep templates modular.

screens.title: CloudFormation vs CDK
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing CloudFormation and CDK helps you pick the right approach for your team. CloudFormation is declarative: you write YAML or JSON templates that describe the final state. It’s explicit, easy to review, and integrates with change sets and drift detection. The CDK is programmatic: you write constructs in languages like TypeScript that synthesize to CloudFormation. CDK reduces boilerplate, lets you create custom constructs to encapsulate a secure pipeline pattern, and enables reuse across projects. A concrete scenario: if your team needs strict, human-reviewable templates for regulated environments, CloudFormation templates with nested stacks and parameters are a strong fit. If you have many similar pipelines and want to share behavior via code, CDK constructs reduce repetition. A common mistake is believing CDK bypasses CloudFormation features; it does not — CDK synthesizes templates and you should still use change sets, drift detection, and IAM reviews. Takeaway: choose CDK for abstraction and reuse and CloudFormation for explicit, template-first governance. Which trade-off matters more in your organization: explicit templates or reusable constructs? CloudFormation vs CDK means cloudformation is explicit and reviewable; cdk is abstract and reusable. both synthesize to the same operational model.. In practical terms, choose declarative templates or programmatic constructs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.5 › CloudFormation vs CDK
CloudFormation

Declarative templates

  • Explicit, easy to audit in templates.
  • Direct support for change sets, outputs, and drift detection.
  • Preferred when strict template review is required.
When to pick
Regulated environments or teams that want direct template control.
AWS CDK

Programmatic constructs

  • Write constructs in TypeScript, Python, Java, or C# and synthesize templates.
  • Encourages reuse and encapsulates best practices as constructs.
  • Reduces boilerplate for large, repeated pipeline patterns.
When to pick
Large organizations with many similar pipelines who want shared constructs and abstraction.
Both approaches end up as CloudFormation templates when applied; CDK simply gives you higher-level language features to generate those templates. Keep using change sets and drift detection as part of your release process regardless of the tool.

Create modular templates

screens.title: Change Sets: Safe Updates
screens.narratorSegment: Change sets give you a preview of how a template update will modify existing resources. Instead of immediately updating a stack, you create a change set which lists resources to be added, modified, or removed. For production pipelines this is vital: it lets reviewers check whether a CodeBuild compute type change, an IAM modification, or an artifact bucket replacement will occur. A concrete workflow is to run aws cloudformation create-change-set with your updated template, review the changes in the console or CLI, and then execute the change set if approved. A typical misconception is thinking change sets always show runtime impact; they show planned resource changes but not application-level effects like longer build times. Use change sets with nested stacks and CDK-generated templates — always synthesize and then create the change set. Takeaway: require change set reviews for production pipeline updates and ensure reviewers understand resource-level and operational impacts. Workflow

Create, review, and execute

  1. Synthesize or prepare the updated template.
  2. Create a change set to compare current and desired states.
  3. Review the list of resource additions, updates, and removals.
  4. Approve and execute the change set or revise the template if needed.

screens.title: Custom Resources and Extensions
screens.narratorSegment: Custom resources let you extend CloudFormation by running custom provisioning logic during stack operations, typically implemented with Lambda functions. For CI/CD you might need to call an external A P I to configure a third-party deployment target or perform complex data transformations that CloudFormation does not support natively. The pattern is to define an AWS::CloudFormation::CustomResource in your template and point it to a Lambda function that implements Create, Update, and Delete handlers. A concrete example is invoking a Lambda to register a webhook or configure a third-party code host as part of pipeline provisioning. A common mistake is making custom resource logic long-running or stateful; keep the Lambda idempotent and ensure it reports success or failure back to CloudFormation. Also secure any credentials used by the function and avoid embedding secrets directly into templates. Takeaway: use custom resources to fill gaps, but keep them small, idempotent, and auditable. Pattern

Lambda-backed custom resources

Define an AWS::CloudFormation::CustomResource that calls a Lambda. The Lambda implements create, update, and delete handlers and signals status back to CloudFormation.

Use case
Registering webhooks or configuring third-party CI integrations that CloudFormation cannot natively manage.
Security note
Do not embed secrets in templates; grant the Lambda the narrowest permissions and store secrets in a secure store referenced by the function.
Checklist
  • Make the Lambda idempotent and fast.
  • Handle failures clearly so CloudFormation can roll back or report errors.
  • Secure any external credentials via managed secrets, not template literals.
Key Takeaway

Custom resources fill functional gaps but require operational discipline: idempotency, security, and clear failure handling.

screens.title: Migrating Manual Pipelines and Drift Detection
screens.narratorSegment: Migrating a manually configured pipeline to IaC requires careful planning to avoid accidental resource deletion. Start by extracting the current configuration using CloudFormation's get-template or tools that can capture resource definitions. For imports, CloudFormation supports importing resources into a stack; plan parameter names and logical IDs carefully so the import maps correctly. After migration, regularly run drift detection to identify resources that differ from the template. For example, if someone changed a CodeBuild compute type in the console, drift detection will flag that property as drifted. Detecting drift lets you decide to update the template to the new desired state or revert the manual change. A common error is relying solely on one-off imports without setting guardrails — follow with policy-as-code and automated drift checks. Takeaway: import with care, run drift detection regularly, and keep the template as the source of truth. Module 02 › Chapter 2.5 › Migration & Drift
Steps
  1. Extract the current configuration with aws cloudformation get-template or equivalent tooling.
  2. Create a CloudFormation template that models the existing resources and plan an import mapping.
  3. Use CloudFormation import to add existing resources to a stack without replacement.
  4. Run drift detection periodically to identify manual changes and resolve by updating code or reverting changes.
Example
If a developer temporarily changes compute type in CodeBuild, run detect-stack-drift to flag that change and then either update the template or revert the console change.
Best practice
  • Run drift detection on a schedule and after manual maintenance windows.
  • Enforce pipeline baselines via policy-as-code and code review.
  • Use change sets and approvals for any updates to production pipeline stacks.
Key Takeaway

Treat the template as the source of truth: import carefully, detect drift, and update the code or revert manual changes consistently.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on treating your CI/CD pipeline itself as code. Infrastructure as Code means you write machine-readable templates that create the very pipelines that build, test, and deploy your applications. You will see how CloudFormation templates define resources like CodeCommit repositories and CodeBuild projects, and how the AWS Cloud Development Kit lets you express the same infrastructure in familiar programming languages. This matters because pipelines that are versioned, reviewed, and deployed from code are reproducible, auditable, and safe to update. A concrete example is a CloudFormation template that creates a CodeCommit repo, an S3 artifacts bucket, an IAM role for builds, and a CodeBuild project with a buildspec provided inline. Common errors come from only putting application infra in IaC while keeping pipelines manual — that causes drift and hidden differences between environments. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to choose a tool, model a pipeline in code, use nested templates or constructs for reuse, and run drift detection to keep resources in sync. Start by comparing CloudFormation's declarative stacks with CDK's programmatic constructs and follow with hands-on templates and a CDK example.

These objectives focus on both declarative and programmatic IaC for CI/CD. First, you'll be able to define and manage AWS CI/CD resources like CodeCommit, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline using CloudFormation templates, which gives you a single source of truth for pipeline provisioning. Second, you'll use the AWS CDK to programmatically define pipelines and their infrastructure. CDK lets you write constructs in languages such as TypeScript or Python and synthesize CloudFormation, reducing boilerplate and improving reuse. Third, you'll implement advanced CloudFormation features such as nested stacks, change sets, and custom resources to build modular, safe pipeline automation. These features matter for safe updates and team workflows. Fourth, you'll migrate manually configured pipelines to IaC and detect drift so your deployed resources match the code. A common misconception is that IaC is only for servers; here we show why pipelines themselves must be managed as code. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify competency by deploying a small pipeline stack and running drift detection.

Beyond knowing the tools, you'll gain practical skills and verification steps. You will be able to author a CloudFormation template that provisions an S3 artifacts bucket, a CodeCommit repository, and a CodeBuild project with IAM roles and buildspec. You will also be able to author a CDK construct that encapsulates a pipeline stage and reuse it across projects. The skills include creating nested stacks to split responsibilities, generating change sets for safe updates, and implementing a Lambda-backed custom resource to extend provisioning. A practical milestone is deploying the ci-cd-infra. yaml example and verifying the resources exist, then running drift detection to confirm no manual changes slipped in. A common misconception is that CDK bypasses CloudFormation — in fact CDK synthesizes templates and still benefits from change sets and drift checks. These learning objectives are deliberately hands-on so you can measure success by deployment, verification, and automated checks.

Infrastructure as Code means expressing infrastructure and automation in machine-readable files so they can be versioned, reviewed, and deployed like software. For CI/CD this extends to the pipeline itself: repositories, build projects, artifact buckets, pipeline stages, and deploy applications are all resources you can manage in code. A clear example is writing a CloudFormation template that creates a CodeCommit repository, an S3 bucket for build artifacts, an IAM role, and a CodeBuild project with a buildspec. Treating these components as code provides repeatability — you can recreate the entire pipeline in a new account — and auditability because changes are visible in Git history. A common misconception is that IaC removes the need for operational review; instead, it shifts review earlier into code review, where change sets and approvals become important. Another contrast is between declaring resources in a static template versus programmatically generating them with CDK; both produce a final template, but CDK encourages reuse through constructs. Takeaway: model pipelines as first-class code artifacts and verify them with deployments and drift detection. How would you enforce a security baseline in every generated pipeline?

CloudFormation lets you declare resources in YAML or JSON templates and manage them as a single unit called a stack. For CI/CD, a stack can include a CodeCommit repository, an S3 artifacts bucket, IAM roles, CodeBuild projects, and CodePipeline definitions. Each template describes the desired state; CloudFormation creates, updates, or deletes resources to match that state. Outputs expose useful values like a repository clone URL or a build project name for use in other stacks or scripts. A concrete example is the provided ci-cd-infra. yaml which creates a CodeCommit repo and a CodeBuild project with a buildspec. Intrinsic functions like reference and get-attribute connect resources inside a stack or nested stacks. A common misconception is that updating a template immediately changes resources; instead you submit a stack update or create a change set to preview changes. Use outputs and parameters to make templates reusable across environments, and prefer named IAM roles and least-privilege policies in templates to reduce risk. Closing question: what outputs would you expose to integrate a stack with another pipeline? CloudFormation: Stacks and templates means a cloudformation stack groups resources so you can manage the full pipeline lifecycle through template changes.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The template sets the project name, a service role for permissions, artifact configuration pointing to an S3 bucket, environment settings such as compute type and image, and a source block that references a CodeCommit repository. Intrinsic functions like get-attribute and reference connect resources: for example the project uses a service role ARN retrieved with get-attribute and points to the artifacts bucket using reference. An example buildspec is often provided either inline or as a file in the repository; this controls phases such as install and build. Intrinsic functions are the glue inside CloudFormation templates that let one resource reference another. Two key functions used in CI/CD templates are reference and get-attribute. Use reference to retrieve a resource's logical name or parameter value, and use get-attribute to fetch properties such as an ARN or a clone URL. For example, a CodeBuild project's Artifacts Location can be set to the bucket name returned by reference, and the project's ServiceRole can be set using get-attribute to retrieve the role's ARN after it is created. These functions matter because they keep templates modular and allow nested stacks to share values without hard-coding names. A common confusion is expecting these functions to return runtime values visible before stack creation; instead they resolve during template processing by CloudFormation. Comparing CloudFormation and CDK helps you pick the right approach for your team. CloudFormation is declarative: you write YAML or JSON templates that describe the final state. It’s explicit, easy to review, and integrates with change sets and drift detection. The CDK is programmatic: you write constructs in languages like TypeScript that synthesize to CloudFormation. CDK reduces boilerplate, lets you create custom constructs to encapsulate a secure pipeline pattern, and enables reuse across projects. A concrete scenario: if your team needs strict, human-reviewable templates for regulated environments, CloudFormation templates with nested stacks and parameters are a strong fit. If you have many similar pipelines and want to share behavior via code, CDK constructs reduce repetition. A common mistake is believing CDK bypasses CloudFormation features; it does not — CDK synthesizes templates and you should still use change sets, drift detection, and IAM reviews. Takeaway: choose CDK for abstraction and reuse and CloudFormation for explicit, template-first governance. Consider a TypeScript stack that creates a code repository, a build project, and a pipeline with source and build stages. Change sets give you a preview of how a template update will modify existing resources. Instead of immediately updating a stack, you create a change set which lists resources to be added, modified, or removed. Custom resources let you extend CloudFormation by running custom provisioning logic during stack operations, typically implemented with Lambda functions. Here are the essential concepts to carry forward. Infrastructure as Code is about managing pipelines in machine-readable templates so they are versioned and repeatable. CloudFormation is the declarative engine that provisions stacks — use parameters, outputs, and intrinsic functions to connect resources. CDK provides programmatic constructs that synthesize to CloudFormation and are useful for reuse and reducing boilerplate. Nested stacks, change sets, and custom resources extend CloudFormation’s power; nested stacks modularize templates, change sets let you preview updates, and custom resources enable functionality not supported natively. Finally, migration and drift detection ensure manually created resources can be absorbed into IaC without losing integrity.
